name: Feeding America: policy, research and awareness (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: Feeding America's US food policy advocacy, research and awareness.
summary: Feeding America's policy and advocacy, research (Map the Meal Gap) and public awareness programmes ($49 million in the year to June 2025) campaign with the rest of the anti-hunger coalition to protect and expand federal food programmes such as SNAP, TEFAP and Summer EBT. Counted as a past average over five years (about $2.5 billion a year of lasting federal food money won or kept, from Summer EBT and the 2025 budget law's smaller SNAP cut), valued for SNAP households net of what it costs the taxpayers who fund it, with a tenth of it caused by the coalition and a quarter of the coalition's resources Feeding America's, and its next dollar at 39% of the average, a dollar does about 0.016 years of healthy life per $1,000. It is far below the global-health median because the money goes to US households only a few times poorer per person than those who pay for it. The result is mostly uncertainty: whether the coalition caused any of the money is a judgment spanning fifteen-fold, and the branch is discounted for missing data.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Feeding America, policy and advocacy, research and public awareness (FY2025)

resources.title: Feeding America, 2025 annual report (fiscal year to 30 June 2025)

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Spending on policy and advocacy, research and analysis and public awareness, FY2025 (year to 30 June 2025)
rows.explainer: The three programme lines that work on public policy and opinion rather than moving food, in Feeding America's own cash (the audited statement of functional expenses before donated goods): policy and advocacy $15.4 million, research and analysis $20.9 million (Map the Meal Gap and the network's data, which the advocacy and the members use), public awareness and education $12.6 million. The $80.7 million of donated media booked to public awareness is the media companies' resource, not Feeding America's cost. Fiscal year 1 July 2024 to 30 June 2025, the same as the food network model (feeding-america-charityevals).

rows.label: Total expenses in cash, net of members' repayments, FY2025
rows.explainer: All cash expenses before donated goods, less the member food banks' repayments for food bought on their behalf (their own money), as in the food network model.

rows.label: Programme expenses in cash, net of members' repayments, FY2025
rows.explainer: All six programme lines in cash, less the members' repayments: the base over which management and fundraising are spread.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads management and fundraising over programs in proportion to their cost, as GiveWell and ACE do.

rows.label: Cost of the advocacy, research and awareness programmes, including overhead
New yearly federal food-assistance money the anti-hunger coalition's wins brought or kept, per year of campaigning (US$ a year)
rows.explainer: A past average over the five years to FY2025, so one year's spending is set against a fifth of what the campaigns won: Summer EBT, made permanent in December 2022 at about $2.5 billion a year; the 2025 budget law's SNAP cut, which Feeding America puts at about $200 billion over ten years against about $300 billion in the House's version, so about $10 billion a year kept (whether the coalition kept it is the counterfactual below); against losses such as USDA's cancellation of $500 million of TEFAP deliveries in 2025. About $12 billion a year over five years: $2.5 billion a year, range $0.5 billion (most of the 2025 difference had other causes) to $8 billion.

source.title: Feeding America, 2025 annual report (fiscal year to 30 June 2025)
source.page: p. 6, Urgent and Effective Advocacy in Action
source.quote: the provisions originally passed in the House cut around $300 billion in benefits (or around 9 billion meals lost per year).

rows.label: Share of the money that reaches households as benefits
rows.explainer: SNAP's benefits are about nine tenths of its federal and state cost; the rest is administration. 0.9, range 0.8 to 0.97.

rows.label: SNAP: average monthly benefit per person, FY2025 (US$)

source.title: Congressional Research Service, SNAP: A Primer on Eligibility and Benefits (R42505, 4 November 2026)
source.quote: Monthly benefits averaged $188.30 per person and $353.43 per household.

rows.explainer: The national average per participant, used to turn the money into people helped for a year.

rows.label: SNAP: benefit per person per year (US$)
People getting a year of benefits from each year's wins
rows.explainer: The yearly money that reaches households over a year's benefit per person: people helped for a year, each year the win lasts.

rows.label: Money moved or raised for other charities in the year modelled (US$)
rows.explainer: 0: the government money the advocacy helps win is valued above as what it does for the people who get it, net of what it costs those who pay, not as money moved. Donations the awareness work brings to food banks are in the unmodelled share.

rows.label: Money moved per dollar of the charity's cost
rows.explainer: Context, and the donors' share of the resources with credit by share of resources on.

rows.label: SNAP households' consumption per person, as a share of the average
rows.explainer: SNAP's gross income limit is 130% of the poverty line, so participants sit in or below the poorest fifth, whose spending per person is about 67% of the average (45% per household, @united_states.ce_lowest_quintile_vs_all_2024, in smaller households); SNAP itself and other benefits are part of their spending. 0.5, range 0.35 to 0.7, a little below the food network model's 0.6 for pantry users, many of whom earn more.

rows.label: SNAP households' consumption per person (US$, household survey)
What a dollar of SNAP is worth to the household against a dollar of cash
rows.explainer: Most households spend more on food than their SNAP benefit, so the benefit frees cash for other things and is worth nearly its face value (Hoynes and Schanzenbach 2009 find food spending responds to SNAP about as to cash). 0.95, range 0.85 to 1.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person per year of benefits
Marginal cost of public funds: what a dollar of public money costs those who pay, in dollars
rows.explainer: Raising a dollar of tax costs the economy more than a dollar through the work and spending it discourages: estimates for rich countries' taxes run from about 1.1 to 1.5 (Dahlby 2008, The Marginal Cost of Public Funds). 1.2, range 1 to 1.5, the same judgment as the Habitat for Humanity advocacy build's and the food network model's.

rows.label: How the federal taxes behind SNAP fall, relative to a tax proportional to consumption
rows.explainer: On the log scale a dollar taken from someone costs 1 over their consumption; a tax proportional to consumption is a multiple of 1, a progressive one above 1. SNAP is federal money, paid by the income tax and borrowing, which fall mostly on richer households: 1.4, range 1 to 2, the same as the food network model's.

rows.label: ln(consumption) given up by those who pay, per person per year of benefits
rows.explainer: The whole cost behind a person's year of benefits (administration included), at the national-accounts consumption per person, times the cost of raising it.

rows.label: Net value per person per year of benefits (units of value)
rows.explainer: What a year of benefits does for a SNAP household on the site's log-income scale, net of what it costs those who pay for it.

rows.label: Gross value per person per year of benefits, before the payers' cost (units of value)
Probability the wins happen, given the work
rows.explainer: 1: the model counts wins that have happened (an average over five years, failures included in the spending); whether they would have come anyway is the counterfactual, asked once (Convention 5).

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (Your values → How impact is counted; docs/normalization.md 2.9). Never the charity's or an evaluator's own years.

rows.label: Wait from the win to when the money reaches households
rows.explainer: Benefit changes take effect at the next fiscal year or within months; Summer EBT took about a year and a half to start. Half a year, range 0 to 2.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact

Value of the money moved (units of value)
Value of a dollar to global health and poverty charities (GiveWell's Top Charities, live), units of value
rows.explainer: GiveWell's four Top Charities (Against Malaria Foundation, Malaria Consortium's seasonal malaria chemoprevention, Helen Keller Intl's vitamin A, New Incentives), each at its result on this site under your values, weighted by what GiveWell directed to each in 2024 (50%, 29%, 18%, 4%).

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, units of value
rows.explainer: This organisation moves money only to global health and poverty charities, so a dollar moved is valued at that destination alone (GiveWell's Top Charities, live).

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: 1× GiveDirectly), units of value
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Shifted money was going to be given anyway; it is credited only for the gain. Where it would have gone is valued at GiveDirectly's live result (GiveWell's model), as Ambitious Impact does, times a shared multiple (1×, from 0 to 3×).

rows.label: Share of money moved that is new money
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for every meta charity: about half the money moved wouldn't otherwise have been given (Ambitious Impact's Effective Giving Incubation report), from 35% to 80%.

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, net of where shifted money would have gone, units of value
rows.explainer: New money counts in full; shifted money counts for the gain over where it would have gone.

rows.label: Careers changed to high-impact work in the year modelled
rows.explainer: 0: the programmes don't aim to move people into other careers.

rows.explainer: Not used: no careers are counted (careers_changed is 0). The template's figure, kept so the shared career rows stay intact.

rows.explainer: Not used: no careers are counted (careers_changed is 0). The template's figure, kept so the shared career rows stay intact.

rows.label: Years a career changer stays, discounted

rows.label: Value of the career changes (units of value)
How much of the money and its reach is real and specific to these wins
rows.explainer: The money figures are the campaigns' own (Summer EBT's cost from budget estimates, the 2025 difference from Feeding America's reading of two bills); part of a 'kept' cut may come back in later laws. 0.7, range 0.4 to 1, near the Habitat advocacy build's US branch (0.6, 0.3 to 0.9), with better-documented federal money.

rows.label: Share of the money that wouldn't have come at all, or not for many years, without the anti-hunger coalition's advocacy
rows.explainer: Most campaigns change nothing, and SNAP's size is set mostly by the parties' majorities and budget rules (the 2025 Senate changes followed parliamentary rulings and senators' own states). 0.1, range 0.02 to 0.3, against the Habitat advocacy build's 0.15 for local housing money, since federal food money moves less with advocacy.

rows.label: Feeding America's share of the resources of the coalition behind the wins
rows.explainer: The anti-hunger coalition: the member food banks' own advocacy, Feeding America Action, the Food Research and Action Center, the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, Share Our Strength, faith groups, and states' agencies. Feeding America is the largest by budget and the voice of the food banks; 0.25, range 0.1 to 0.5.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: no measured outcome for Feeding America's advocacy; the money, its reach and the share caused are judgments from the campaigns' own figures and the research on advocacy.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of the households' gross value
rows.explainer: Not modelled, as a share of the households' gross value: (+) the awareness campaigns and donated advertising bring donations and volunteers to food banks, +2%; (+) Map the Meal Gap and the network's data help food banks put food where need is greatest, +2%; (+) wins that carry no money (school meal rules, SNAP access for students), +1%; (-) benefits that reduce work a little, -0%. 5%, range -5% to +20%.

rows.label: Total units of value
rows.formula: downstream_value * total_adj + unmodelled_benefits_adj * gross_value * total_adj + moved_value + careers_value
rows.explainer: The net value of the wins after Feeding America's share and the adjustments, plus the unmodelled share of the households' gross value.

rows.label: Value per dollar
rows.explainer: For WELLBYs, rename the uov_* rows to wellbys_* and report in wellby. For animals, rename them to sads_* and add the species section of the corporate-campaign template (output ced_per_donor_dollar). For climate, start from the climate skeleton.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of the programmes' cost
rows.explainer: The three lines' own salaries and benefits over their cash spending (34%), Feeding America's figure in place of the shared default (Convention 1).

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: The shared gap for advocacy staff: policy, research and campaign staff could earn more in lobbying or consulting.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff (in-kind donation)
